title: Baptism
hook: water poured three times in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word sacrament: an outward sign that does what it shows. Your line was signs that do something. Which small sign did you mean all the way? Day one hundred twenty-six.

Sunday afternoon, at the back of a church. A baby in a white outfit that took three people to get onto her. Grandparents with phones up. A godmother holding a candle a little too close to her hair. The priest takes a small shell or a jug, and pours water over the baby's forehead, once, twice, three times, saying the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The baby is often furious about it. Everyone else is smiling. Catholics believe something enormous just happened, in a few seconds. Today, the first sacrament: baptism.
screen: `A BABY IN WHITE.` → `WATER, THREE TIMES.` → `A FEW SECONDS, SOMETHING ENORMOUS.`

segments.voice: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo, to dip, plunge or immerse. Some churches baptize by going right under the water; others pour, and the Catholic Church allows both. Either way, the sign is the same: washing, going under, coming up. Jesus himself was baptized by John in the Jordan. And at the end of Matthew's Gospel he sends his followers out with this, in the Douay-Rheims: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." That's where the three names come from, and the three pourings follow them. What do Catholics believe baptism does? The Catechism names a lot: sins washed away, a new birth as a child of God, membership in the Church, and a mark on the soul that can never be undone, which is why a person is baptized only once. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one enters the kingdom of God unless born again of water and the Spirit. So Catholics call it a birth. Some Catholics keep the date, like a birthday: a first birthday of another kind. And no baby comes alone. Godparents promise to help raise the child in the faith. In many Hispanic families they're padrinos, and the parents and godparents become compadres, family for life. In many Filipino families they're ninong and ninang, and there are often several. Two surprising facts. In an emergency, anyone can baptize, even someone who isn't Christian, by pouring water and saying those words with the intention of doing what the Church does. And the Catholic Church recognizes baptisms in other Christian churches when they're done with water and those same three names. Christians do differ on when: Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Anglicans and others baptize babies, while Baptists and others baptize only those old enough to profess faith themselves.
screen: `BAPTIZO: TO DIP, TO PLUNGE.` · `IN THE NAME OF FATHER, SON, SPIRIT.` · `A NEW BIRTH, ONCE, FOR GOOD.` · `ANYONE CAN BAPTIZE IN AN EMERGENCY.` · then, large: `BORN AGAIN OF WATER AND THE SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember your water, or someone's. Settle, and breathe. If you were baptized, you probably don't remember it. Think instead of who was there: who held you, who promised things on your behalf. If you weren't, think of a baptism you've seen, or simply of water: the first splash of a morning shower, rain on your face. Notice it. If you pray, you can thank God for the people who carried you. Later, try to find the date. The bell holds the time.
Baptism. From the Greek for dipping under. Water poured three times in the three names, and Catholics believe, a second birth. Today's word.

Your line: your first birthday. This week: the luminous, sorrowful and glorious mysteries, the Salve Regina, one decade a day, sacrament, and now baptism. Today, find out your baptism date, or ask someone theirs. Day one hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics are usually baptized as babies: the priest or deacon pours water over the head three times in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, with godparents promising to help raise the child in the faith.

original.note: Greek: to dip, plunge or immerse.

trapdoor: what you thought: a naming ceremony for babies.
what it means: the first sacrament: water and the three names, which Catholics believe make a person a child of God, once and for good.
what a scholar hears: baptizo, to immerse; the Trinitarian formula of Matthew 28:19, and a baptism the Catholic Church recognizes in other churches when done with water and the three names.

notes: Emergency baptism by anyone, even a non-baptized person, with the right intention: CCC 1256. Confirm.
Recognition of other churches' baptisms (water + Trinitarian formula): generally true; some groups' baptisms are not recognized. Script says 'most'. Confirm.
Indelible character, baptism once: CCC 1272. Confirm.
Immersion vs pouring: both permitted in the Latin rite. Confirm.
